<result># XCUITest Suite Survey — `macapp/WorkroomAppUITests/`

**Scope:** 37 source files, 38 executed `XCTestCase` classes (36 concrete files + `VCSToolbarUITestsBase`, an abstract base with zero runs of its own, executed twice via its two concrete subclasses `VCSToolbarGitUITests`/`VCSToolbarJJUITests`), **215 individual test-method executions**, **~227 real app-process launches** (215 base, +7 from `AgentResumeUITests` doing 2 launches per test, +6 from `SessionRestoreUITests`' quit/relaunch pairs, −1 for `DiffHighlightUITests.testRubyDiffIsHighlighted`, which `XCTSkip`s before ever calling `launchedApp()`). Every test method calls its own `launchedApp()` helper — there is no shared/reused app instance across test methods anywhere in the suite, so the launch count above is close to the true CPU/wall-time cost driver.

One infra note up front so it isn't relitigated: **parallelizing this suite is not a safe lever.** `WorkroomApp/Core/UITestFixture.swift` documents that `-parallel-testing` workers are separate processes sharing one on-disk `UserDefaults` domain, so one worker's test can silently corrupt another's read mid-run ("a class holding the key true for the length of a test body silently early-returns another class's history refresh, in a worker whose diff has nothing to do with any of this"). The path to a faster suite is fewer/cheaper launches, not more concurrent ones.

---

## Ranked cut/consolidation list (ranked by launches-saved × confidence)

### 1. `VCSToolbarUITests.swift` — de-duplicate the git/jj backend parameterization (≈18 launches saved, high confidence)
`/Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom/macapp/WorkroomAppUITests/VCSToolbarUITests.swift`

`VCSToolbarUITestsBase` declares 20 tests once; `VCSToolbarGitUITests` and `VCSToolbarJJUITests` each run all 20 → **40 launches for 20 unique test bodies.** Only two of the 20 (`testBranchSegmentShowsTheCurrentRefAndItsBackendNoun`, `testCaptionAlwaysRendersAndTheSegmentIsNotAControl`) assert anything that actually differs between backends (the "Branch" vs "Bookmark" noun). The other 18 — every sync-state test, the push/pull/fetch seam tests, the failure-dialog tests — exercise the same SwiftUI view against the same backend-agnostic `FixtureVCSWriter`/seeded `VCSRemoteState`; nothing in their assertions is backend-shaped.

There's a second, independent reason to cut, stated in the file's own header: **"The jj suite needs a real `jj` ≥ 0.43 on PATH… on a machine with jj missing or too old the sync segment correctly disables itself and the state tests fail."** So 20 of the 40 launches are also coupled to an external tool-version dependency that has nothing to do with the behavior most of them test. `/Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom/macapp/WorkroomAppTests/VCSSyncPresentationTests.swift` exists and, per the file header's own claim, already covers "the variant ordering and the backend vocabulary" at unit level.

**Recommendation:** keep only the two noun-sensitive tests parameterized (4 launches); move the other 18 to a single git-only class. **Net: 40 → 22 launches**, and 18 tests stop depending on a jj install.

### 2. `AgentResumeUITests.swift` + `SessionRestoreUITests.swift` — scope out of routine runs, don't delete (≈29 of ~227 total launches, i.e. ~13% of the whole suite from 2 files)
`/Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom/macapp/WorkroomAppUITests/AgentResumeUITests.swift` (7 tests, **14 launches** — every test does a quit+relaunch cycle)
`/Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom/macapp/WorkroomAppUITests/SessionRestoreUITests.swift` (9 tests, **15 launches** — 6 tests quit+relaunch, 3 launch once)

These are the two most expensive files per-test in the suite (each real launch here pays for a fresh shell boot, at least one real quit, and a second fresh boot). Both files' own doc comments already say "Run on a GUI login session: `make app-uitest`, or scoped via `xcodebuild -only-testing`" — i.e., the repo already tells you to scope these rather than run them in the default sweep. That's the existing guidance to lean on, not a new one to invent.

**Do not cut** `AgentResumeUITests.testWithNoSeededRootDiscoveryIsANoOp` or `SessionRestoreUITests.testWithoutASessionPathNothingIsWritten` despite looking like weak "nothing happened" assertions — they are the suite's **isolation tripwires**. `UITestFixture.swift` states outright that without default-off `agentSessionRoot`, "the existing UI tests would read the DEVELOPER's real `~/.claude`," and without default-off `sessionFilePath`, "the 30-odd existing UI tests would each write over the DEVELOPER's own `Workroom Dev` session." Losing these removes the guard that keeps every *other* test in the suite hermetic — keep, with this reasoning attached.

The 7 `AgentResumeUITests` tests are individually not reducible either: the claude-only and codex-only tests each prove *exclusivity* (that seeding one agent's history does NOT also offer the other's button), which the both-agents test can't show on its own.

**One concrete, safe merge within `SessionRestoreUITests`:** `testSplitSurvivesRelaunch` and `testTabCountSurvivesRelaunchWithNoStrayTerminal` both just do "mutate state → quit → relaunch → assert a count." Build a split **and** extra tabs before the one quit, assert both pane-count and tab-count after the one relaunch. **Saves 1 full 2-launch cycle.**

**Recommendation:** exclude both files from the routine/full sweep via `-only-testing` exclusion (or a separate "slow" scheme), run them on a slower cadence (pre-release / nightly), keep all tests as-is otherwise.

### 3. Trivially-subsumed single-assertion tests (4 launches saved, high confidence — each is one full launch to prove something another test in the same file already exercises as a side effect)

- `NewWindowUITests.testNewWindowMenuItemPresent` — `/Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom/macapp/WorkroomAppUITests/NewWindowUITests.swift` — asserts the menu item exists; `testNewWindowOpensBlankSecondWindow` in the same file *clicks* that exact item, which necessarily proves it exists too. Cut the standalone existence test.
- `NewWorkroomDialogUITests.testNewWorkroomMenuItemPresentAndEnabled` — `/Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom/macapp/WorkroomAppUITests/NewWorkroomDialogUITests.swift` — same shape; `testDialogOpensListsAndFiltersProjects` clicks the same item and gets the dialog open. Cut.
- `SettingsSidebarUITests.testAboutPaneHasUpdateControlsAndLinks` — `/Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom/macapp/WorkroomAppUITests/SettingsSidebarUITests.swift` — `testClickingEachSidebarRowSwitchesTheDetailPane` already clicks into the About pane and asserts `about.checkForUpdates`. Fold this test's four remaining id checks (`about.version`, `about.repo`, `about.releaseNotes`, `settings.control.releaseChannel`) into that existing About-pane visit instead of a second full launch.
- `WorkroomsViewUITests.testActiveWorkroomShowsATab` — `/Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom/macapp/WorkroomAppUITests/WorkroomsViewUITests.swift` — the file's *only* test, asserting a `workroom.tab.*` element exists on launch. This exact precondition is already required (and therefore proven) by `WindowDragUITests` and every `TabStripOverflowUITests`/`TabStripScrollIntoViewUITests` test, which all wait on a workroom chip before doing anything else. **Cutting this removes the entire file/class** (1 launch, 0 unique signal).

### 4. `TabStripOverflowUITests.testChromeGlyphButtonsAreHittableWhenInline` + `…WhenPinned` — fold into `testChromeGlyphButtonsClaimTheirWholeWell` (2 launches saved, high confidence)
`/Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom/macapp/WorkroomAppUITests/TabStripOverflowUITests.swift`

Both tests exist to re-disprove a finding that `TODOS.md` (line ~2604) already closed: *"Chrome glyph buttons' `isHittable == false`" — closed as an environmental XCUITest artefact, not an a11y defect; nothing in the app was wrong.* Line ~2617 explains why: `isHittable` is accessibility hit-testing, which can't distinguish a genuinely broken control from a covering window/backgrounded state — so it is structurally the wrong check to keep asserting. The app-specific half of what these tests intend to protect (real on-screen frame, inside the window, not collapsed to a point) is already independently covered by `testChromeGlyphButtonsClaimTheirWholeWell` and the geometry tests (`testAddTabButtonStaysVisibleWhenTabsOverflow`, `testPinnedAddButtonKeepsGutterFromToolbar`, `testWorkroomBarControlsStayVisibleWhenChipsOverflow`). This is squarely the "asserting framework/OS-level behavior" pattern the task called out.

### 5. `WindowDragUITests.testDraggingWorkroomTabReordersTwoChips` — documented flake, isolate rather than run in the default batch
`/Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom/macapp/WorkroomAppUITests/WindowDragUITests.swift`

`TODOS.md` ("`WindowDragUITests.testDraggingWorkroomTabReordersTwoChips` is a known gesture-timing flake") records a reproduced pass-then-fail on two **identical back-to-back reruns of the identical binary** during the beta.24 release gate — a coin-flip test, by the project's own record. It also costs real wall time on top of that: the drag is deliberately synthesized `withVelocity: .slow, thenHoldForDuration: 0.5`. Not a pure cut candidate (it's the only test proving the reorder gesture works at all), but it should not be in the routine/full-suite path where its ~50% flake rate costs a rerun or a false red. Recommend a dedicated retry wrapper or isolating it to a "known-flaky" scheme rather than deleting.

### 6. `DiffHighlightUITests.testRubyDiffIsHighlighted` — dead code, delete (0 runtime cost, but inflates the count)
`/Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom/macapp/WorkroomAppUITests/DiffHighlightUITests.swift`

Immediately throws `XCTSkip` before calling `launchedApp()` — it never launches the app and costs no wall time, so it isn't a *speed* fix, but it is a "test" that runs nothing and never will (SwiftUI's async `@State` highlight write has no observable a11y-changed notification for XCUITest, per the method's own doc). Real coverage already lives in `DiffHighlightMapperTests.testFixtureRubyDiffPipelineProducesHighlightedLines` (unit, per the same doc). Delete the method rather than leave a permanent skip in the UI target.

### 7. Lower-priority consolidation opportunities (medium confidence, smaller individual savings)

- **`ViewMenuShortcutsUITests.swift`** (`/Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom/macapp/WorkroomAppUITests/ViewMenuShortcutsUITests.swift`) — 8 tests, each a full launch to flip one shortcut. Four are literal `…WithTerminalFocused`/`…WithoutTerminalFocused` pairs testing the same shortcut (Projects ⌃⌘S, OS-standard ⌥⌘S, secondary ⌥⌘B). Nothing stops testing both focus states inside one launched instance (click a terminal, test, then click off it and test again) — could cut this file's launches from 8 to ~4.
- **`SplitPaneUITests.testTwoSplitGroupsBothPersistAcrossSelection`** + **`testEachSplitGroupBracketFramesItsOwnChips`** (`/Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom/macapp/WorkroomAppUITests/SplitPaneUITests.swift`) — both launch the identical expensive 3-workroom/2-split-group fixture. Combine into one test asserting bracket geometry and cross-group persistence together. Saves 1 launch.
- **`StatusBarCwdUITests.swift`**'s two tests (`/Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom/macapp/WorkroomAppUITests/StatusBarCwdUITests.swift`) both wait up to 20s for a real OSC-7 cwd report before doing anything — combine into one launch (open menu, assert both items, click Copy, assert pasteboard). Saves 1 launch (and ~20s of shared wait).
- **`NewWorkroomDialogUITests.waitForFileMenuItemEnabled`** (same file as above) busy-loops opening/reading/Escaping the File menu with **no sleep between iterations**, for up to 8s, to observe `@FocusedValue` republication timing. Not removable — it's testing a real async race — but it's a real wall-time/thrash cost signal (repeated menu-open/close animations) worth a small floor delay rather than a tight spin.

### 8. Keep, but exclude from full/CI-batch runs — `HistoryStressUITests.testLargeHistoryStaysInteractive`
`/Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom/macapp/WorkroomAppUITests/HistoryStressUITests.swift`

Asserts a hard **2.0-second** wall-clock budget for opening a changeset from an 800-row synthetic page — deliberately tight ("a budget under the 2000ms app-hang threshold, so a stalled main thread fails instead of passing slowly"). That's exactly the shape the task calls out: a timing assertion that is more likely to trip from contention (CPU shared with 200+ other launches in a serial batch run) than from a real regression. The file's own doc comment already says "Run per-method: `xcodebuild … -only-testing:…/HistoryStressUITests/<method>`" — an explicit, pre-existing instruction to scope it rather than fold it into the full sweep. Keep it as a standalone perf regression check for the WORKROOM-2B hang fix; don't run it in the default batch.

---

## Exhaustive per-file inventory (all 37 files)

Each entry: test names — what's exercised — cost signal.

**`ActivityBarDirtyDotUITests.swift`** (1 test, 1 launch) — `testChangesIconShowsDirtyForDirtyWorkroom`: dirty workroom → Changes icon's a11y *value* says "has changes," no peer icon inherits it. Cheap, unique signal, keep.

**`ActivityBarUITests.swift`** (3, 3) — icon-click swaps Changes/Files pane content; clicking the active icon collapses it; History collapses in place inside the Changes stack. Distinct, cheap. Keep.

**`AgentResumeUITests.swift`** (7 tests, 14 launches) — see ranked item #2. Real quit/relaunch + filesystem-seeded Claude/Codex session discovery + a real typed-and-submitted `claude --resume` in a live PTY. Highest per-test cost in the suite. Scope out of routine runs; keep all tests.

**`ChangesPanelUITests.swift`** (6, 6) — jj working-copy flat header/file-list rendering; bookmark renders once (toolbar) not twice (header); conflicted-file badge (positive+negative control); sidebar aggregate conflict dot on collapse; in-app "Open File" renders real seeded content. All distinct, moderate cost. Keep.

**`ChangesetDetailUITests.swift`** (6, 6) — History row → changeset detail tab; double-click persists vs. single-click previews; History empties when tabs close; divergence disclosure reveals siblings; renamed-file "old → new" row; root() row renders inert. Distinct, no unit-test substitute (real click-through + real accessibility tree combining). Keep.

**`CommitSheetUITests.swift`** (13, 13) — commit dialog seam: file checkboxes (git) vs. none (jj); blocked-until-summary; count tracks deselection; select-all; per-backend second verb (Amend vs Describe); render-cap vs. real commit count; amend-target naming; rejected-commit keeps sheet+hook output; success closes sheet; cancel discards. Largest "legit" file by test count but low internal overlap — each test is a distinct button/state seam. `testASuccessfulCommitClosesTheSheet`/`testCancelClosesTheSheetWithoutCommitting` are the cheapest pair here and could in principle share a launch, but they test opposite outcomes of the same click, so keep separate.

**`DiffHighlightUITests.swift`** (3, 2 launches — 1 is dead) — Ruby diff highlight test is a permanent `XCTSkip` (see #6, delete); deletion lines never highlighted; unknown-language diffs render plain. Keep the two real tests.

**`DiffPaneFocusUITests.swift`** (1, 1) — regression: clicking a terminal pane focuses it even when a diff pane was focused (AppKit responder-chain bug, not reachable from a unit test). Keep, unique.

**`DiffViewerUITests.swift`** (7, 7) — jj `@` vs git worktree diff source; single-click preview retargets in place; row selection follows focus; double-click persists and coexists with a later preview; side-by-side two-column rendering; per-tab diff-mode toggle overrides the global default. Each proves a distinct interaction; legitimate XCUITest territory (real click-through + tab-state). Keep.

**`GhosttyActionDispatchUITests.swift`** (2, 2) — `SET_TITLE`/`PROGRESS_REPORT` libghostty action dispatch via a real PTY + real shell integration/OSC. Explicitly NOT unit-testable per its own doc (only observable side effect for an engine-internal enum). Cost: `sleep 6`/two `sleep 5`s inside the driven shell commands (~6–10s of intentional wait per test) — justified, this is exactly the "only a real terminal proves this" case. Keep.

**`GhosttyCLIUITests.swift`** (1, 1) — `GHOSTTY_BIN_DIR` / `ghostty` symlink / `+ssh-cache` dispatch, all through a real shell. Already model-citizen behavior: its own doc says "Three questions, one app launch… they share all of its setup" — a good example of consolidation already done right. Keep as-is; nothing to cut.

**`HistoryPushStateUITests.swift`** (4, 4) — exactly-one-badge suppression proof across `@`/pushed/unknown/divergent-sibling rows; changeset header states/omits the unpushed marker. Precise count-based assertions, not reproducible from a unit test (rendering + suppression rules together). Keep.

**`HistoryStressUITests.swift`** (4, 4) — see item #8 for `testLargeHistoryStaysInteractive`. The other three (realizes-only-visible-rows, scroll-away-and-back, off-screen row opens its own changeset) are the WORKROOM-2B lazy-list regression proof and have no substitute. File already self-documents "run per-method." Keep all four, exclude from full-batch runs.

**`InspectorAnimationUITests.swift`** (1, 1) — collapsing a section moves the next header up/back via real accessibility-geometry frames. Cheap, unique (geometry can't be asserted headlessly). Keep.

**`MarkdownPreviewUITests.swift`** (4, 4) — loader shown while WKWebView boots; loader disappears on render; whole-file rendering past a raw `<title>` mention (real truncation regression); raw `<title>` renders as visible text not markup. All distinct WKWebView-rendering assertions no unit test can see. Keep.

**`NavigationHistoryContentUITests.swift`** (1, 1) — `⌘[`/`⌘]` return the PANE (not just the sidebar) to a previous diff — the specific bug was about pane content, so a store-level test couldn't have caught it. Keep.

**`NewWindowUITests.swift`** (3, 3) — menu item present (cut, see #3); new window opens blank; new window matches existing window's size. Cost signal: `Thread.sleep(1.5)` and `Thread.sleep(1.0)` fixed sleeps rather than polled waits — works, but is dead wall time and a minor flake risk if window-settle timing ever grows past 1.5s. Consider converting to a polled wait.

**`NewWorkroomDialogUITests.swift`** (10, 10) — menu item present+enabled (cut, see #3); disabled-with-no-projects; title-bar buttons render with no tabs; dialog lists/filters projects; five "shortcut inert while dialog is up, then works after" tests (⌘T, ⌘1, text-editing keys, typing routes to dialog not terminal, title-bar Open button inert); shortcut doesn't reach a non-key workroom window. The five "inert-then-works" tests are legitimately distinct regressions (different shortcuts/routes, per issue #128-adjacent work) but share near-identical shape; moderate consolidation opportunity, lower priority than the item-4 cuts above. `waitForFileMenuItemEnabled`'s no-sleep busy loop (item #7) lives here.

**`PullRequestWarningUITests.swift`** (4, 4) — `gh` unusable-state copy: too-old / not-authenticated / not-installed(+install link) / no-warning-when-not-seeded. Each is a distinct branch of what used to be a broken ternary chain (bug motivated). File already self-documents `-only-testing` scoping. Keep.

**`RunSettingsPromptUITests.swift`** (3, 3) — ⌘R with no run command opens Project Settings with a warning; same via the header Run button click; plain "Project Settings…" context-menu entry shows no warning banner. Each covers a genuinely different entry point into the same sheet (issue #127). Keep; low individual cost.

**`RunStatusUITests.swift`** (3, 3) — real non-zero exit → failed icon; clean exit → no failed icon; in-pane ⌃C → stop, not failure. All three drive a REAL run command via a real PTY (`sleep 1; exit 7`, etc.) — the exact "libghostty child-exit code is unreliable" seam a unit test can't reach. Keep.

**`SessionRestoreUITests.swws`** — see ranked item #2 (14/15... actually 15 launches across 9 tests). Also worth flagging: `testCorruptScrollbackSidecarStillLaunches` and `testCorruptSessionFileStillLaunchesCleanly` are narrow one-off degradation checks (a specific corrupt-file class each) — legitimate but classic "regression test for a narrow bug"; each is already about as cheap as this file gets (1–2 launches), so not worth cutting, just noting the pattern.

1. **`VCSToolbarUITests.swift`** — biggest win. Base class declares 20 tests, run twice (git+jj) = 40 launches for 20 unique bodies. Repo already documents "run scoped, not in full sweep" for these. **Recommendation: exclude from routine/CI sweep via `-only-testing` exclusion, run nightly/pre-release. Do NOT delete tests — `testWithNoSeededRootDiscoveryIsANoOp`/`testWithoutASessionPathNothingIsWritten` are isolation tripwires that keep the rest of the suite hermetic (prevent tests from touching real `~/.claude` or the dev session file).**

<result># Survey: Swift Unit Tests in `macapp/WorkroomAppTests` (XCUITest target `WorkroomAppUITests` excluded per instructions)

**Scope covered:** 147 `*Tests.swift` files, 2,258 test methods (2,257 passed / 1 skipped), all under `/Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom/macapp/WorkroomAppTests/`. I pulled a real `xcresult` bundle sitting in `macapp/DerivedData/Logs/Test/` (`Test-WorkroomApp-2026.08.12_14-02-45-+0100.xcresult`) and extracted **measured per-test durations** via `xcrun xcresulttool`, rather than guessing cost from static patterns. That changes the conclusion substantially from what a naive count-of-tests survey would say.

## Headline finding: test count is the wrong lever here

Sum of all 2,258 measured durations = **183.0s**. That total is **not evenly distributed** — it's dominated by a small number of pathological tests/classes, and the ~2,100 pure-logic tests spread across ~110 files (including the three largest files by test count — `VCSWritingTests` at 123 tests, `WorkroomStatusResolverTests` at 91, `RunCommandTests` at 76) are collectively cheap. Cutting those buys almost nothing. The repo-root `Makefile` itself already says this explicitly:

> "the suite is dominated by a few slow integration classes (Markdown WebView renders, real git/jj repos), so spreading classes across worker processes cuts the run ~40% (48s → ~29s)"

That's also why "speeding up parallelism" stalled: **XCTest parallelizes per class, not per test** (confirmed independently by `SharedPrefDefaultsTests`' own doc comment), so wall-clock floor = the slowest single class. Finding #1 below explains exactly why that floor hasn't been movable.

---

## Finding #1 (fix this first — ~33% of total suite time, one line)

**File:** `WorkroomAppTests/WorkroomStatusTests.swift`
**Test:** `WorkroomStatusTests.testCancelledGitHubCLIProbePublishesNothing()`
**Measured cost:** **60.085s** — by far the single most expensive test in the entire suite (the xcresult's own "Longest Test Runs" insight flags 3 outlier tests covering 38% of total duration; this one test alone is ~33%).

What it does: spins up a `GatedGHRunner` stub whose `run()` does `try? await Task.sleep(nanoseconds: 60_000_000_000)` (60s) until cancelled, then cancels the wrapping `Task` and awaits `task.value`, asserting the store's `githubCLIStatus` wasn't mutated by the cancelled probe.

**Why it costs the full 60s every single run:** `GitHubAuthCache` is deliberately single-flight (by design, per its own header comment) — multiple callers coalesce onto one shared underlying probe. Cancelling *this test's* wrapper `Task` does not cancel the shared in-flight probe task, so `await task.value` blocks until the shared task actually finishes — i.e., the full hardcoded 60-second sleep, unconditionally, on every run, whether in CI or locally. The test's own comment ("long enough that the test's own deadline fails first if cancellation never propagates") assumed cancellation *would* propagate quickly; it structurally can't, given the single-flight design it's testing against.

**Recommendation — fix, don't cut:** the assertion is legitimate and worth keeping (real regression: `refreshGitHubCLI`'s guard against a cancelled probe stomping a good cached value). Just shrink `GatedGHRunner`'s sleep from 60s to ~1–2s (still far longer than the 2s poll window used to detect probe entry) or stop blocking on `task.value` and instead poll `githubCLIStatus` for a bounded window as the test already does for probe-entry. Either change is a 1-line diff, preserves 100% of the signal, and removes ~60s from every single `make app-test` invocation — bigger than every other finding in this report combined.

---

## Finding #2 (second-highest leverage — shared anti-pattern, ~14s, restructure not cut)

**Files:** `ChangedFileRowInvalidationTests.swift` (3 tests, 6.87s measured), `HistoryRowInvalidationTests.swift` (6 tests, 6.19s), `DiffViewerLazyRenderingTests.swift` (3 tests, 1.32s)

All three define an identical `settle(_ view: NSView, seconds: TimeInterval = 0.6)` helper:
```swift
private func settle(_ view: NSView, seconds: TimeInterval = 0.6) {
  let deadline = Date().addingTimeInterval(seconds)
  while Date() < deadline {
    view.layoutSubtreeIfNeeded()
    RunLoop.current.run(until: Date().addingTimeInterval(0.02))
  }
  view.layoutSubtreeIfNeeded()
}
```
This is a **fixed-duration busy-wait, not an early-exit poll** — it always burns the full `seconds` argument regardless of how quickly SwiftUI actually converges. `ChangedFileRowInvalidationTests.testSelectionChangeRebuildsChangedFileRows` calls it 3 times (1.2s + 0.6s + 0.6s = 2.4s guaranteed minimum), which matches its measured 3.095s almost exactly.

**Recommendation — restructure, keep the assertion:** these are legitimate regression nets for real App Hangs (WORKROOM-2B/2T/2S, named in the doc comments) and the assertions themselves (`bodyPasses` counts) are good — this isn't the kind of test to delete. Replace the fixed busy-wait with a poll-until-condition-or-ceiling (check the actual `bodyPasses`/render-settled signal each spin iteration and `return` early), keeping the same `seconds` value only as a safety-net ceiling. Typical cost drops from "always pays 0.6–1.2s" to "pays whatever SwiftUI actually needs," likely cutting this ~14.4s cluster by 70–90% with zero loss of regression coverage. `PaneRenderingTests.swift` and `HistoryCommitCardTests.swift` use the same offscreen-NSWindow-hosting harness pattern (per their own doc cross-references) — worth checking whether they duplicate the same fixed-wait pattern in the same pass.

---

## Finding #3: real git/jj integration classes — legitimate two-tier coverage, but consolidate the fixture cost

These files spawn real `git`/`jj` subprocesses against real throwaway repos (`/bin/sh -c` `Process()` calls), verified via grep counts and measured durations:

| File | Tests | Measured total | `sh()` calls | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `VCSRemoteIntegrationTests.swift` | 23 | 18.13s | 74 (14× `gitFixture()`, 9× `jjFixture()`) | fetch/push/pull against real bare repos |
| `VCSProviderConformanceTests.swift` | 12 | 12.33s | 20 | colocated jj+git cross-backend conformance |
| `WorkroomStatusIntegrationTests.swift` | 32 | 10.87s | 51 | porcelain-v2/jj-template parsing vs. real binaries |
| `GitCommitDiffTests.swift` | 15 | 8.56s | 18 | raw libgit2 rename/typechange/shallow-boundary reads |
| `VCSCommitIntegrationTests.swift` | 21 | 6.42s | 30 | `CLIVCSWriter.commit` against real repos |
| `GitGraphTests.swift` | 11 | 4.67s | 13 | push-state graph walk via raw libgit2 |

Together: **114 tests, ~61s (≈33% of total suite time)**, each test independently builds a fresh git/jj repo from scratch via `gitFixture()`/`jjFixture()` helpers (each ~6–7 real process spawns just to set up).

**These are not low-value duplicates** — each file's header explicitly states the two-tier rationale ("the unit tests pin the parsing; this proves the two halves meet") and several tests exist specifically because a prior *unit*-level fix shipped a real bug the unit test couldn't see (documented per-test, e.g. `testFetchAtTheRootMovesAWorkroomsLastFetchLabel`, `testRenameCommitsBothSides`). This is the disciplined kind of two-tier coverage the task asked me to distinguish from actual duplication — I'm not recommending cuts here.

**Recommendation — consolidate fixture setup, not test count:** within `VCSRemoteIntegrationTests`, several tests build near-identical `gitFixture()`/`jjFixture()` bases and then diverge by one appended git/jj operation (e.g. `testBehindIsCountedAfterTheRemoteMovesOn` and `testDivergedCountsBothDirections` both clone-push-fetch from the same base shape). Where the *assertions* don't depend on isolation from each other (no shared mutable state risk), collapsing sibling scenarios into one test with multiple assertions against one built fixture (as `testCountsAreIdenticalUnderEveryPushDefault` already does, looping 5 `push.default` values against a single fixture) would cut a meaningful fraction of the ~9 `jjFixture()` calls (each ~7 process spawns) without losing any single regression signal. Two specific outlier single tests worth flagging but *not* worth chasing further: `GitCommitDiffTests.testShallowBoundaryCommitListsItsFilesAsAdded` (5.4s — inherent cost of a real `file://` shallow-clone transport negotiation, needed to test that specific libgit2/grafts interaction) and `VCSProviderConformanceTests.testColocatedPushStateMatchesAcrossBackends` (5.8s — colocated jj+git init is expensive by nature). Both are isolated, correctly-scoped, low-priority.

`StatusCommandRunnerTests.swift` (15 tests, 4.4s) and `ShellEnvironmentTests.swift` (36 tests, 3.7s) also spawn real processes, but these are testing this app's own process-lifecycle code (SIGTERM/SIGKILL grace, PATH probing, stdin nulling, cancellation-doesn't-block-the-caller) — this is exactly the kind of thing that *cannot* be tested without a real process, so **no removal recommendation**; the cost is inherent to what's being verified.

---

## Finding #4: genuine framework-behavior / near-duplicate candidates (small runtime, but real "cut" candidates per your criteria)

These are cheap in wall time (sub-10ms each) but match your explicit "testing the framework, not our logic" and "duplicate coverage" criteria, so I'm flagging them as clean, low-risk cuts even though they won't move the runtime needle:

- **`ConfirmOnCloseTerminalTests.swift`** (class `ConfirmOnCloseTerminalTests`, 4 tests) and **`CopyOnSelectTests.swift`** (class `CopyOnSelectTests`, 2 tests) — both assert that a `Defaults.Key` declared with `default: true` returns `true` when the underlying `UserDefaults` key is absent. That's testing the `Defaults` library's own default-value contract, not app logic; the two files are near-duplicates of each other in shape. **Recommend: cut to a single shared test (or delete both) — the `Key`'s declaration is the actual guarantee, and a compiler-checked default doesn't need a runtime regression test per call site.**
- **`SettingsPaneTests.swift`** (5 tests) and **`ActivitySectionTests.swift`** (8 tests, partial) — both assert "`allCases` is declared in this literal order" (a change-detector comparing a hardcoded list against itself) plus "an unrecognized raw string falls back to the default case," which is `Defaults` + `PreferRawRepresentable`'s behavior, exercised against a private probe key. **Recommend: keep the fallback test (it does guard a real corruption/rename scenario per the doc), cut the bare `allCases`-order assertion** — a reorder is caught by any test that depends on section ordering elsewhere, and if nothing else depends on it, the order isn't actually load-bearing.

## Finding #5: exhaustive-enumeration tests — flagged per your criteria, but honestly near-zero runtime cost

**File:** `SwitcherThemeSweepTests.swift` (5 tests, sweeping all 116 bundled ghostty themes) — this is structurally exactly the "iterate every X" pattern you asked me to flag, and its own doc comment concedes "two fixtures can't answer this" as the justification for going exhaustive. **But measured cost is 0.13s total across all 5 tests** (pure in-memory color-math over static theme data — no I/O, no process spawns). Similarly `GhosttyResourcesTests.testBundledResourceChecksumsMatch` and `ThemeServiceTests.testBundledThemeChecksumsMatch` (golden-checksum-style tests) each cost under 20ms. **Recommendation: do not touch these for runtime reasons — cutting them saves ~0.15s out of 183s.** If the team wants fewer assertions for maintainability/signal-noise reasons independent of speed, `SwitcherThemeSweepTests` could reasonably shrink to the adversarial subset its own doc already names (near-monochrome theme, ANSI-blue-near-background theme, pale-accent light theme) with the full 116-theme sweep moved to an opt-in/manual tier — but this is a maintainability call, not a speed one.

# Plan: cut test-suite runtime — defect fixes + genuine superfluous-test cuts

## Context

Test suite is slow. Prior attempt to speed it up at the infra/parallelism level failed, so the
ask was to instead find tests that are superfluous, unnecessary, or testing something this app
doesn't actually provide, and cut/consolidate those.

Three parallel Explore agents surveyed the Go CLI tests, the macapp Swift unit tests, and the
macapp XCUITest suite. I then verified their highest-impact claims by reading the actual source
(not just trusting agent summaries) — several claims didn't hold up and are corrected below,
because a review's value is worthless if the recommendations are wrong.

**The real finding: the slowness is mostly two defects, not superfluous tests.** Once verified,
the genuine "cut because it's unnecessary" list is small. The user chose to include the defect
fixes in this plan too (confirmed via question), since they dominate the actual runtime by far.
The user also chose to skip measuring the XCUITest suite directly (would require real app
launches, ~30-40 min for a full run) and use launch-count as the cost proxy instead — confirmed
this matches the measured ~9s/launch average (30-40 min / ~227 launches).

## Three cost mechanisms found, ranked by impact

### A. `WorkroomStatusTests.testCancelledGitHubCLIProbePublishesNothing` — 60s of 183s (33% of the whole macapp unit suite)

**File:** `macapp/WorkroomAppTests/WorkroomStatusTests.swift:877-978`

`GatedGHRunner.run()` (line 975) does `try? await Task.sleep(nanoseconds: 60_000_000_000)`.

### Handling 5+ options — split, never drop

AskUserQuestion caps every call at **4 options**. With 5+ real options, NEVER
drop, merge, or silently defer one to fit. Pick a compliant shape:

- **Batch into ≤4-groups** — for coherent alternatives (e.g. version bumps,
  layout variants). One call, 5th surfaced only if first 4 don't fit.
- **Split per-option** — for independent scope items (e.g. "ship E1..E6?").
  Fire N sequential calls, one per option. Default to this when unsure.

Per-option call shape: `D<N>.k` header (e.g. D3.1..D3.5), ELI10 per option,
Recommendation, kind-note (no completeness score — Include/Defer/Cut/Hold are
decision actions), and 4 buckets:
**A) Include**, **B) Defer**, **C) Cut**, **D) Hold** (stop chain, discuss).

After the chain, fire `D<N>.final` to validate the assembled set (reprompt
dependency conflicts) and confirm shipping it. Use `D<N>.revise-<k>` to
revise one option without re-running the chain.

For N>6, fire a `D<N>.0` meta-AskUserQuestion first (proceed / narrow / batch).

question_ids for split chains: `<skill>-split-<option-slug>` (kebab-case ASCII,
≤64 chars, `-2`/`-3` suffix on collision). The runtime checker
(`bin/gstack-question-preference`) refuses `never-ask` on any `*-split-*` id,
so split chains are never AUTO_DECIDE-eligible — the user's option set is sacred.

**Full rule + worked examples + Hold/dependency semantics:** see
`docs/askuserquestion-split.md` in the gstack repo. Read on demand when N>4.

**Non-ASCII characters — write directly, never \u-escape.** When any string
field contains Chinese (繁體/簡體), Japanese, Korean, or other non-ASCII text,
emit the literal UTF-8 characters; never escape them as `\uXXXX` (the pipe is
UTF-8 native, and manual escaping miscodes long CJK strings). Only `\n`,
`\t`, `\"`, `\\` remain allowed. Full rationale + worked example: see
`docs/askuserquestion-cjk.md`. Read on demand when a question contains CJK.

### Self-check before emitting

Before calling AskUserQuestion, verify:
- [ ] D<N> header present
- [ ] ELI10 paragraph present (stakes line too)
- [ ] Recommendation line present with concrete reason
- [ ] Completeness scored (coverage) OR kind-note present (kind)
- [ ] Every option has ≥2 ✅ and ≥1 ❌, each ≥40 chars (or hard-stop escape)
- [ ] (recommended) label on one option (even for neutral-posture)
- [ ] Dual-scale effort labels on effort-bearing options (human / CC)
- [ ] Net line closes the decision
- [ ] You are calling the tool, not writing prose — unless `CONDUCTOR_SESSION: true` (then prose is the DEFAULT, not the tool) OR the documented failure fallback applies (then: prose with the mandatory triad — issue ELI10, per-choice Completeness, Recommendation + `(recommended)` — and a "reply with a letter" instruction, then STOP)
- [ ] Non-ASCII characters (CJK / accents) written directly, NOT \u-escaped
- [ ] If you had 5+ options, you split (or batched into ≤4-groups) — did NOT drop any
- [ ] If you split, you checked dependencies between options before firing the chain
- [ ] If a per-option Hold fires, you stopped the chain immediately (didn't queue)

The following nudges are tuned for the claude model family. They are
**subordinate** to skill workflow, STOP points, AskUserQuestion gates, plan-mode

## Voice

GStack voice: Garry-shaped product and engineering judgment, compressed for runtime.

- Lead with the point. Say what it does, why it matters, and what changes for the builder.
- Be concrete. Name files, functions, line numbers, commands, outputs, evals, and real numbers.
- Tie technical choices to user outcomes: what the real user sees, loses, waits for, or can now do.
- Be direct about quality. Bugs matter. Edge cases matter. Fix the whole thing, not the demo path.
- Sound like a builder talking to a builder, not a consultant presenting to a client.
- Never corporate, academic, PR, or hype. Avoid filler, throat-clearing, generic optimism, and founder cosplay.
- No em dashes. No AI vocabulary: delve, crucial, robust, comprehensive, nuanced, multifaceted, furthermore, moreover, additionally, pivotal, landscape, tapestry, underscore, foster, showcase, intricate, vibrant, fundamental, significant.
- The user has context you do not: domain knowledge, timing, relationships, taste. Cross-model agreement is a recommendation, not a decision. The user decides.

Good: "auth.ts:47 returns undefined when the session cookie expires. Users hit a white screen. Fix: add a null check and redirect to /login. Two lines."
Bad: "I've identified a potential issue in the authentication flow that may cause problems under certain conditions."

## Writing Style (skip entirely if `EXPLAIN_LEVEL: terse` appears in the preamble echo OR the user's current message explicitly requests terse / no-explanations output)

Applies to AskUserQuestion, user replies, and findings. AskUserQuestion Format is structure; this is prose quality.

## Completeness Principle — Boil the Ocean

AI makes completeness cheap, so the complete thing is the goal. Recommend full coverage (tests, edge cases, error paths) — boil the ocean one lake at a time. The only thing out of scope is genuinely unrelated work (rewrites, multi-quarter migrations); flag that as separate scope, never as an excuse for a shortcut.

When options differ in coverage, include `Completeness: X/10` (10 = all edge cases, 7 = happy path, 3 = shortcut). When options differ in kind, write: `Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.` Do not fabricate scores.

**Embed the question_id as a marker in the question text** so hooks can identify it deterministically (plan-tune cathedral T14 / D18 progressive markers). Append `<gstack-qid:{question_id}>` somewhere in the rendered question (the leading line or trailing line is fine; the marker doesn't render visibly to the user when wrapped in HTML-style angle brackets, but the hook strips it). * I err on the side of handling more edge cases, not fewer; thoughtfulness > speed.
* Bias toward explicit over clever.
* Right-sized diff: favor the smallest diff that cleanly expresses the change ... but don't compress a necessary rewrite into a minimal patch. If the existing foundation is broken, say "scrap it and do this instead."

## Cognitive Patterns — How Great Eng Managers Think

These are not additional checklist items. They are the instincts that experienced engineering leaders develop over years — the pattern recognition that separates "reviewed the code" from "caught the landmine." Apply them throughout your review.

1. **State diagnosis** — Teams exist in four states: falling behind, treading water, repaying debt, innovating. Each demands a different intervention (Larson, An Elegant Puzzle).
2. **Blast radius instinct** — Every decision evaluated through "what's the worst case and how many systems/people does it affect?"
3. **Boring by default** — "Every company gets about three innovation tokens." Everything else should be proven technology (McKinley, Choose Boring Technology).
4. **Incremental over revolutionary** — Strangler fig, not big bang. Canary, not global rollout. Refactor, not rewrite (Fowler).
5. **Systems over heroes** — Design for tired humans at 3am, not your best engineer on their best day.
6. **Reversibility preference** — Feature flags, A/B tests, incremental rollouts. Make the cost of being wrong low.
7. **Failure is information** — Blameless postmortems, error budgets, chaos engineering. Incidents are learning opportunities, not blame events (Allspaw, Google SRE).
8. **Org structure IS architecture** — Conway's Law in practice. Design both intentionally (Skelton/Pais, Team Topologies).
9. **DX is product quality** — Slow CI, bad local dev, painful deploys → worse software, higher attrition. Developer experience is a leading indicator.
10. **Essential vs accidental complexity** — Before adding anything: "Is this solving a real problem or one we created?" (Brooks, No Silver Bullet).
11. **Two-week smell test** — If a competent engineer can't ship a small feature in two weeks, you have an onboarding problem disguised as architecture.
12. **Glue work awareness** — Recognize invisible coordination work. Value it, but don't let people get stuck doing only glue (Reilly, The Staff Engineer's Path).
13. **Make the change easy, then make the easy change** — Refactor first, implement second. Never structural + behavioral changes simultaneously (Beck).
14. **Own your code in production** — No wall between dev and ops. "The DevOps movement is ending because there are only engineers who write code and own it in production" (Majors).
15. **Error budgets over uptime targets** — SLO of 99.9% = 0.1% downtime *budget to spend on shipping*. Reliability is resource allocation (Google SRE).

When evaluating architecture, think "boring by default." When reviewing tests, think "systems over heroes." When assessing complexity, ask Brooks's question. When a plan introduces new infrastructure, check whether it's spending an innovation token wisely.

## Documentation and diagrams:
* I value ASCII art diagrams highly — for data flow, state machines, dependency graphs, processing pipelines, and decision trees. Use them liberally in plans and design docs.
* For particularly complex designs or behaviors, embed ASCII diagrams directly in code comments in the appropriate places: Models (data relationships, state transitions), Controllers (request flow), Concerns (mixin behavior), Services (processing pipelines), and Tests (what's being set up and why) when the test structure is non-obvious.
* **Diagram maintenance is part of the change.** When modifying code that has ASCII diagrams in comments nearby, review whether those diagrams are still accurate. Update them as part of the same commit. Stale diagrams are worse than no diagrams — they actively mislead. Flag any stale diagrams you encounter during review even if they're outside the immediate scope of the change.

   into the appendix so reviewers can audit calibration, but the user does NOT
   see it in the critical-pass output. Do not work around this by inventing
   speculative confidence 7+ — that defeats the gate.

**Framework-meta nudge:** When the symbol is generated by a framework
metaclass, descriptor, ORM Meta inner-class, or migration history (Django
`Meta`, Rails `has_many`/`scope`, SQLAlchemy `relationship`/`Column`,
TypeORM decorators, Sequelize `init`/`belongsTo`, Prisma generated client),
quote the meta-construct (the `Meta` block, the migration, the decorator,
the schema file) instead of expecting the literal name in the class body.
The verification is "I read the source that creates this symbol", not "I
grep'd for the name and didn't find it." Deeper framework-aware verification
(model introspection, migration-history-aware checks, ORM dialect detection)
is deliberately out of scope for the lighter gate — see the deferred
`~/.gstack-dev/plans/1539-framework-aware-review.md` design doc.

The FP classes the gate kills (measured against Django Sprint 2.5 #1539):

| FP class | Why the gate catches it |
|---|---|
| "field doesn't exist on model" | Requires quoting the model class body or Meta; the field's absence becomes obvious |
| "dict.get() might be None" | Requires quoting the dict initialization (e.g. Django form's `cleaned_data` is `{}`-initialized) |
| "save() might lose fields" | Requires quoting the ORM signature or model definition |
| "update_fields might miss X" | Requires quoting the field set; if X doesn't exist, the FP is self-evident |

**Calibration learning:** If you report a finding with confidence < 7 and the user
confirms it IS a real issue, that is a calibration event. Your initial confidence was
too low. Log the corrected pattern as a learning so future reviews catch it with
higher confidence.

### 3. Test review

100% coverage is the goal. Evaluate every codepath in the plan and ensure the plan includes tests for each one. If the plan is missing tests, add them — the plan should be complete enough that implementation includes full test coverage from the start.

### Test Framework Detection

Before analyzing coverage, detect the project's test framework:

1. **Read CLAUDE.md** — look for a `## Testing` section with test command and framework name. If found, use that as the authoritative source.
2. **If CLAUDE.md has no testing section, auto-detect:**

```bash
setopt +o nomatch 2>/dev/null || true  # zsh compat
# Detect project runtime
[ -f Gemfile ] && echo "RUNTIME:ruby"
[ -f package.json ] && echo "RUNTIME:node"
[ -f requirements.txt ] || [ -f pyproject.toml ] && echo "RUNTIME:python"
[ -f go.mod ] && echo "RUNTIME:go"
[ -f Cargo.toml ] && echo "RUNTIME:rust"
# Check for existing test infrastructure
ls jest.config.* vitest.config.* playwright.config.* cypress.config.* .rspec pytest.ini phpunit.xml 2>/dev/null
ls -d test/ tests/ spec/ __tests__/ cypress/ e2e/ 2>/dev/null
```

3. **If no framework detected:** still produce the coverage diagram, but skip test generation.

**Step 1. Trace every codepath in the plan:**

Read the plan document. For each new feature, service, endpoint, or component described, trace how data will flow through the code — don't just list planned functions, actually follow the planned execution:

1. **Read the plan.** For each planned component, understand what it does and how it connects to existing code.
2. **Trace data flow.** Starting from each entry point (route handler, exported function, event listener, component render), follow the data through every branch:
   - Where does input come from? (request params, props, database, API call)
   - What transforms it? (validation, mapping, computation)
   - Where does it go? (database write, API response, rendered output, side effect)
   - What can go wrong at each step? (null/undefined, invalid input, network failure, empty collection)
3. **Diagram the execution.** For each changed file, draw an ASCII diagram showing:
   - Every function/method that was added or modified
   - Every conditional branch (if/else, switch, ternary, guard clause, early return)
   - Every error path (try/catch, rescue, error boundary, fallback)
   - Every call to another function (trace into it — does IT have untested branches?)
   - Every edge: what happens with null input? Empty array? Invalid type?

This is the critical step — you're building a map of every line of code that can execute differently based on input. Every branch in this diagram needs a test.

**Step 2. Map user flows, interactions, and error states:**

Code coverage isn't enough — you need to cover how real users interact with the changed code. For each changed feature, think through:

- **User flows:** What sequence of actions does a user take that touches this code? Map the full journey (e.g., "user clicks 'Pay' → form validates → API call → success/failure screen"). Each step in the journey needs a test.
- **Interaction edge cases:** What happens when the user does something unexpected?
  - Double-click/rapid resubmit
  - Navigate away mid-operation (back button, close tab, click another link)
  - Submit with stale data (page sat open for 30 minutes, session expired)
  - Slow connection (API takes 10 seconds — what does the user see?)
  - Concurrent actions (two tabs, same form)
- **Error states the user can see:** For every error the code handles, what does the user actually experience?
  - Is there a clear error message or a silent failure?
  - Can the user recover (retry, go back, fix input) or are they stuck?
  - What happens with no network? With a 500 from the API? With invalid data from the server?
- **Empty/zero/boundary states:** What does the UI show with zero results? With 10,000 results? With a single character input? With maximum-length input?

Add these to your diagram alongside the code branches. A user flow with no test is just as much a gap as an untested if/else.

**Step 3. Check each branch against existing tests:**

Go through your diagram branch by branch — both code paths AND user flows. For each one, search for a test that exercises it:
- Function `processPayment()` → look for `billing.test.ts`, `billing.spec.ts`, `test/billing_test.rb`
- An if/else → look for tests covering BOTH the true AND false path
- An error handler → look for a test that triggers that specific error condition
- A call to `helperFn()` that has its own branches → those branches need tests too
- A user flow → look for an integration or E2E test that walks through the journey
- An interaction edge case → look for a test that simulates the unexpected action

Quality scoring rubric:
- ★★★  Tests behavior with edge cases AND error paths
- ★★   Tests correct behavior, happy path only
- ★    Smoke test / existence check / trivial assertion (e.g., "it renders", "it doesn't throw")

### E2E Test Decision Matrix

When checking each branch, also determine whether a unit test or E2E/integration test is the right tool:

**RECOMMEND E2E (mark as [→E2E] in the diagram):**
- Common user flow spanning 3+ components/services (e.g., signup → verify email → first login)
- Integration point where mocking hides real failures (e.g., API → queue → worker → DB)
- Auth/payment/data-destruction flows — too important to trust unit tests alone

**RECOMMEND EVAL (mark as [→EVAL] in the diagram):**
- Critical LLM call that needs a quality eval (e.g., prompt change → test output still meets quality bar)
- Changes to prompt templates, system instructions, or tool definitions

**STICK WITH UNIT TESTS:**
- Pure function with clear inputs/outputs
- Internal helper with no side effects
- Edge case of a single function (null input, empty array)
- Obscure/rare flow that isn't customer-facing

### REGRESSION RULE (mandatory)

**IRON RULE:** When the coverage audit identifies a REGRESSION — code that previously worked but the diff broke — a regression test is added to the plan as a critical requirement. No AskUserQuestion. No skipping. Regressions are the highest-priority test because they prove something broke.

A regression is when:
- The diff modifies existing behavior (not new code)
- The existing test suite (if any) doesn't cover the changed path
- The change introduces a new failure mode for existing callers

When uncertain whether a change is a regression, err on the side of writing the test.

**Step 4. Output ASCII coverage diagram:**

Include BOTH code paths and user flows in the same diagram. Mark E2E-worthy and eval-worthy paths:

```

[+] src/services/billing.ts                           [+] Payment checkout

  │   ├── [★★★ TESTED] happy + declined + timeout      ├── [GAP] [→E2E] Double-click submit

  │   └── [GAP]         Invalid currency

LLM integration: [GAP] [→EVAL] Prompt template change — needs eval test
```

Legend: ★★★ behavior + edge + error  |  ★★ happy path  |  ★ smoke check
[→E2E] = needs integration test  |  [→EVAL] = needs LLM eval

**Fast path:** All paths covered → "Test review: All new code paths have test coverage ✓" Continue.

**Step 5. Add missing tests to the plan:**

For each GAP identified in the diagram, add a test requirement to the plan. Be specific:
- What test file to create (match existing naming conventions)
- What the test should assert (specific inputs → expected outputs/behavior)
- Whether it's a unit test, E2E test, or eval (use the decision matrix)
- For regressions: flag as **CRITICAL** and explain what broke

The plan should be complete enough that when implementation begins, every test is written alongside the feature code — not deferred to a follow-up.

## CRITICAL RULE — How to ask questions
Follow the AskUserQuestion format from the Preamble above. Additional rules for plan reviews:
* **One issue = one AskUserQuestion call.** Never combine multiple issues into one question.
* Describe the problem concretely, with file and line references.
* Present 2-3 options, including "do nothing" where that's reasonable.
* For each option, specify in one line: effort (human: ~X / CC: ~Y), risk, and maintenance burden. If the complete option is only marginally more effort than the shortcut with CC, recommend the complete option.
* **Map the reasoning to my engineering preferences above.** One sentence connecting your recommendation to a specific preference (DRY, explicit > clever, minimal diff, etc.).
* Label with issue NUMBER + option LETTER (e.g., "3A", "3B").
* **Coverage vs kind:** for every per-issue AskUserQuestion you raise in this review, decide whether the options differ in coverage or in kind. If coverage (e.g., more tests vs fewer, complete error handling vs happy-path-only, full edge-case coverage vs shortcut), include `Completeness: N/10` on each option. If kind (e.g., architectural choice between two different systems, posture-over-posture, A/B/C where each is a different kind of thing), skip the score and add one line: `Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.` Do NOT fabricate scores on kind-differentiated questions — filler scores are worse than no score.
* **Zero findings:** if a section has zero findings, state "No issues, moving on" and proceed. Otherwise, use AskUserQuestion for each finding — a finding with an "obvious fix" is still a finding and still needs user approval before any change lands in the plan.

### Worktree parallelization strategy

Analyze the plan's implementation steps for parallel execution opportunities. This helps the user split work across git worktrees (via Claude Code's Agent tool with `isolation: "worktree"` or parallel workspaces).

**Skip if:** all steps touch the same primary module, or the plan has fewer than 2 independent workstreams. In that case, write: "Sequential implementation, no parallelization opportunity."

**Otherwise, produce:**

1. **Dependency table** — for each implementation step/workstream:

| Step | Modules touched | Depends on |
|------|----------------|------------|
| (step name) | (directories/modules, NOT specific files) | (other steps, or —) |

Work at the module/directory level, not file level. Plans describe intent ("add API endpoints"), not specific files. Module-level ("controllers/, models/") is reliable; file-level is guesswork.

2. **Parallel lanes** — group steps into lanes:
   - Steps with no shared modules and no dependency go in separate lanes (parallel)
   - Steps sharing a module directory go in the same lane (sequential)
   - Steps depending on other steps go in later lanes

Format: `Lane A: step1 → step2 (sequential, shared models/)` / `Lane B: step3 (independent)`

3. **Execution order** — which lanes launch in parallel, which wait. Example: "Launch A + B in parallel worktrees. Merge both. Then C."

4. **Conflict flags** — if two parallel lanes touch the same module directory, flag it: "Lanes X and Y both touch module/ — potential merge conflict. Consider sequential execution or careful coordination."

Measured on throwaway repos. Fix: --pathspec-from-file=- with --pathspec-file-nul (paths taken literally, also removes argv E2BIG), or a :(literal) prefix per path. Related: `git commit -- <path>` implies --only and DISCARDS staged content for that path (data loss after git add -p), and --only alone cannot commit an untracked file, so a preceding `git add` is mandatory. jj is worse: paths are a fileset EXPRESSION language, a space hard-fails to parse, and a fileset matching nothing still creates an empty commit and exits 0.

1	# Plan: cut test-suite runtime — defect fixes + genuine superfluous-test cuts
2	
3	## Context
4	
5	Test suite is slow. Prior attempt to speed it up at the infra/parallelism level failed, so the
6	ask was to instead find tests that are superfluous, unnecessary, or testing something this app
7	doesn't actually provide, and cut/consolidate those.
8	
9	Three parallel Explore agents surveyed the Go CLI tests, the macapp Swift unit tests, and the
10	macapp XCUITest suite. I then verified their highest-impact claims by reading the actual source
11	(not just trusting agent summaries) — several claims didn't hold up and are corrected below,
12	because a review's value is worthless if the recommendations are wrong.
13	
14	**The real finding: the slowness is mostly two defects, not superfluous tests.** Once verified,
15	the genuine "cut because it's unnecessary" list is small. The user chose to include the defect
16	fixes in this plan too (confirmed via question), since they dominate the actual runtime by far.
17	The user also chose to skip measuring the XCUITest suite directly (would require real app
18	launches, ~30-40 min for a full run) and use launch-count as the cost proxy instead — confirmed
19	this matches the measured ~9s/launch average (30-40 min / ~227 launches).
20	
21	## Three cost mechanisms found, ranked by impact
22	
23	### A. `WorkroomStatusTests.testCancelledGitHubCLIProbePublishesNothing` — 60s of 183s (33% of the whole macapp unit suite)
24	
25	**File:** `macapp/WorkroomAppTests/WorkroomStatusTests.swift:877-978`
26	
27	`GatedGHRunner.run()` (line 975) does `try? await Task.sleep(nanoseconds: 60_000_000_000)`.
28	`GitHubAuthCache`/the probe machinery is deliberately single-flight, so cancelling the test's
29	wrapper `Task` does NOT cancel the shared in-flight probe — `await task.value` (line 892) blocks
30	until the full 60s sleep actually finishes, every single run, in CI or locally. Verified by
31	reading the full test body and the runner double — the mechanism is exactly as measured.
32	
33	**Fix:** shrink the sleep to ~2-3s (still comfortably longer than the 2s poll-for-entry window
34	the test itself uses at line 886-889 to detect the probe has started). Update the stale comment
35	at line 973-974 ("long enough that the test's own deadline fails first if cancellation never
36	propagates") to match the new duration/margin — leaving it unchanged after the sleep shrinks
37	would misdocument the safety margin for the next person who touches this file. The assertion
38	(`store.githubCLIStatus` unchanged after cancellation) is legitimate and must be kept exactly as
39	is — this is a real regression guard (header comment: "the false, sticky 'GitHub CLI not signed
40	in'" bug), just do not shrink the sleep so much it races the runner's own `enteredGHProbe` gate.
41	
42	**Impact: saves ~57-58s of the 183s macapp unit suite. Bigger than every other finding in this
43	plan combined.** Also explains why parallelism work didn't help — XCTest parallelizes per class,
44	and a hardcoded 60s sleep inside one class floors that class's wall-clock regardless of how many
45	workers run alongside it.
46	
47	### B. Fixed-duration `settle()` busy-wait helper, duplicated across 4 files (~17-20s)
48	
49	**Files (verified via grep, one more than the original survey found):**
50	- `macapp/WorkroomAppTests/ChangedFileRowInvalidationTests.swift`
51	- `macapp/WorkroomAppTests/HistoryRowInvalidationTests.swift`
52	- `macapp/WorkroomAppTests/DiffViewerLazyRenderingTests.swift`
53	- `macapp/WorkroomAppTests/AgentResumeCoordinatorTests.swift` (not in the original survey — found by grepping `func settle` across the test dir; same anti-pattern, called ~6 times with a 0.5s default)
54	
55	Each defines a private `settle(seconds:)` that busy-waits a FIXED duration regardless of how fast
56	the thing being waited on actually converges:
57	```swift
58	private func settle(_ view: NSView, seconds: TimeInterval = 0.6) {
59	  let deadline = Date().addingTimeInterval(seconds)
60	  while Date() < deadline {
61	    view.layoutSubtreeIfNeeded()
62	    RunLoop.current.run(until: Date().addingTimeInterval(0.02))
63	  }
64	  view.layoutSubtreeIfNeeded()
65	}
66	```
67	This always pays the full `seconds` argument — it's not a poll-until-condition with an early
68	exit, it's a poll-until-timeout. `ChangedFileRowInvalidationTests` alone calls it 3x for a
69	guaranteed 2.4s minimum, matching its measured 3.1s almost exactly.
70	
71	**Fix:** keep the assertions (these are real regression nets for named App Hangs —
72	WORKROOM-2B/2T/2S per the doc comments, cross-referenced in project memory
73	`macapp-focus-responder-apphang-2t.md`), but change each `settle()` to poll the actual
74	convergence signal each spin (e.g. the `bodyPasses` counter each file already tracks stops
75	incrementing) and return as soon as it's stable, keeping `seconds` only as a safety ceiling.
76	**Impact: cuts this cluster from "always pays the full duration" to "pays what SwiftUI actually
77	needs," likely 70-90% of ~17-20s.** `RunCommandTests.swift` and `RemoteStateModelTests.swift` also
78	define a `settle()`, but verified those use bounded `XCTestExpectation`/async patterns for a
79	deliberate dwell-time assertion, not the busy-wait anti-pattern — leave those alone.

103	  (`cmd/delete_project_integration_test.go:140`) both `t.Skip` when `jj` isn't on PATH, and the
104	  `cli` CI job never installs `jj` — these never run in CI today, only for a dev with jj installed

1	# Plan: cut test-suite runtime — defect fixes + genuine superfluous-test cuts
2	
3	## Context
4	
5	Test suite is slow. Prior attempt to speed it up at the infra/parallelism level failed, so the
6	ask was to instead find tests that are superfluous, unnecessary, or testing something this app
7	doesn't actually provide, and cut/consolidate those.
8	
9	Three parallel Explore agents surveyed the Go CLI tests, the macapp Swift unit tests, and the
10	macapp XCUITest suite. I then verified their highest-impact claims by reading the actual source
11	(not just trusting agent summaries) — several claims didn't hold up and are corrected below,
12	because a review's value is worthless if the recommendations are wrong.
13	
14	**The real finding: the slowness is mostly two defects, not superfluous tests.** Once verified,
15	the genuine "cut because it's unnecessary" list is small. The user chose to include the defect
16	fixes in this plan too (confirmed via question), since they dominate the actual runtime by far.
17	The user also chose to skip measuring the XCUITest suite directly (would require real app
18	launches, ~30-40 min for a full run) and use launch-count as the cost proxy instead — confirmed
19	this matches the measured ~9s/launch average (30-40 min / ~227 launches).
20	
21	## Three cost mechanisms found, ranked by impact
22	
23	### A. `WorkroomStatusTests.testCancelledGitHubCLIProbePublishesNothing` — 60s of 183s (33% of the whole macapp unit suite)
24	
25	**File:** `macapp/WorkroomAppTests/WorkroomStatusTests.swift:877-978`
26	
27	`GatedGHRunner.run()` (line 975) does `try? await Task.sleep(nanoseconds: 60_000_000_000)`.
28	`GitHubAuthCache`/the probe machinery is deliberately single-flight, so cancelling the test's
29	wrapper `Task` does NOT cancel the shared in-flight probe — `await task.value` (line 892) blocks
30	until the full 60s sleep actually finishes, every single run, in CI or locally. Verified by
31	reading the full test body and the runner double — the mechanism is exactly as measured.
32	
33	**Fix:** shrink the sleep to ~2-3s (still comfortably longer than the 2s poll-for-entry window
34	the test itself uses at line 886-889 to detect the probe has started). Update the stale comment
35	at line 973-974 ("long enough that the test's own deadline fails first if cancellation never
36	propagates") to match the new duration/margin — leaving it unchanged after the sleep shrinks
37	would misdocument the safety margin for the next person who touches this file. The assertion
38	(`store.githubCLIStatus` unchanged after cancellation) is legitimate and must be kept exactly as
39	is — this is a real regression guard (header comment: "the false, sticky 'GitHub CLI not signed
40	in'" bug), just do not shrink the sleep so much it races the runner's own `enteredGHProbe` gate.
41	
42	**Impact: saves ~57-58s of the 183s macapp unit suite. Bigger than every other finding in this
43	plan combined.** Also explains why parallelism work didn't help — XCTest parallelizes per class,
44	and a hardcoded 60s sleep inside one class floors that class's wall-clock regardless of how many
45	workers run alongside it.
46	
47	### B. Fixed-duration `settle()` busy-wait helper, duplicated across 4 files (~17-20s)
48	
49	**Files (verified via grep, one more than the original survey found):**
50	- `macapp/WorkroomAppTests/ChangedFileRowInvalidationTests.swift`
51	- `macapp/WorkroomAppTests/HistoryRowInvalidationTests.swift`
52	- `macapp/WorkroomAppTests/DiffViewerLazyRenderingTests.swift`
53	- `macapp/WorkroomAppTests/AgentResumeCoordinatorTests.swift` (not in the original survey — found by grepping `func settle` across the test dir; same anti-pattern, called ~6 times with a 0.5s default)
54	
55	Each defines a private `settle(seconds:)` that busy-waits a FIXED duration regardless of how fast
56	the thing being waited on actually converges:
57	```swift
58	private func settle(_ view: NSView, seconds: TimeInterval = 0.6) {
59	  let deadline = Date().addingTimeInterval(seconds)
60	  while Date() < deadline {
61	    view.layoutSubtreeIfNeeded()
62	    RunLoop.current.run(until: Date().addingTimeInterval(0.02))
63	  }
64	  view.layoutSubtreeIfNeeded()
65	}
66	```

- The `settle()` redesign is not specified enough to be safe. “Counter stops incrementing” is not convergence; it may only mean the delayed invalidation has not arrived yet. Early return could turn hang regressions into false passes. Each call site needs a proven completion signal, not a generic stability guess.

- The 17–20s saving is therefore speculative. The fixed dwell may be part of what detects repeated invalidation. Until the replacement is mutation-tested against the actual historical failure modes, the claimed saving is unsupported.

- The shared helper’s proposed unit tests only verify timer mechanics. They do not prove that layout/run-loop pumping observes delayed SwiftUI work or catches the regressions these four tests exist for.

- Adding `Support/Settle.swift` may require Xcode target/project membership. The plan assumes automatic source discovery and omits any possible `.xcodeproj` change.

- The 60s test should not retain an arbitrary 2–3s sleep. Use a controllable continuation/gate: detect entry, cancel, release the probe immediately with a result, then assert it was not published. The proposed fix preserves the same timing smell and a fixed multi-second floor.

- The XCUITest arithmetic is wrong. `testRubyDiffIsHighlighted` skips before launching the app, so deleting it saves no launch and no meaningful runtime. The claimed “~6 launches/~1 min” overstates the cut.

- Changing `make app-uitest` to silently omit 29 launches is not test optimization; it redefines the default suite as partial. Since XCUITest has no CI or nightly execution, “runnable with `APP_UITEST_FLAGS=`” effectively means those tests may never run or will rot.

- Skipping the isolation tripwires in the routine run is especially poorly calibrated. The plan itself says they guard against touching developer-owned state, then removes them from the path developers normally execute.

- “Isolate to a flaky/retry lane” is not implemented anywhere. No target, script, CI job, or file change creates such a lane for `testDraggingWorkroomTabReordersTwoChips`. That recommendation is orphaned.

- A cryptic empty-variable override is not an adequate full-suite workflow. If partial execution is intentional, it needs explicit `app-uitest-fast`, `app-uitest-full`, and flaky/retry targets, with some enforced cadence for the full run.

- Verification contradicts the decision to avoid a full 30–40 minute UI run: step 6 explicitly runs the full suite via `APP_UITEST_FLAGS=`. It also does not verify the proposed flaky lane because none exists.

- “Downstream test requires the element” is weaker than true subsumption unless it uses the same fixture and directly fails on that precondition. The plan assumes equivalence across different UI-test classes without establishing identical launch state.

- The performance estimates rely on one aggregate duration and launch count. There is no repeated baseline, variance, or per-test post-change comparison. A claimed 70–90% reduction in asynchronous UI tests needs measurement, not extrapolation.

THE PLAN:
# Plan: cut test-suite runtime — defect fixes + genuine superfluous-test cuts

## Context

Test suite is slow. Prior attempt to speed it up at the infra/parallelism level failed, so the
ask was to instead find tests that are superfluous, unnecessary, or testing something this app
doesn't actually provide, and cut/consolidate those.

Three parallel Explore agents surveyed the Go CLI tests, the macapp Swift unit tests, and the
macapp XCUITest suite. I then verified their highest-impact claims by reading the actual source
(not just trusting agent summaries) — several claims didn't hold up and are corrected below,
because a review's value is worthless if the recommendations are wrong.

**The real finding: the slowness is mostly two defects, not superfluous tests.** Once verified,
the genuine "cut because it's unnecessary" list is small. The user chose to include the defect
fixes in this plan too (confirmed via question), since they dominate the actual runtime by far.
The user also chose to skip measuring the XCUITest suite directly (would require real app
launches, ~30-40 min for a full run) and use launch-count as the cost proxy instead — confirmed
this matches the measured ~9s/launch average (30-40 min / ~227 launches).

## Three cost mechanisms found, ranked by impact

### A. `WorkroomStatusTests.testCancelledGitHubCLIProbePublishesNothing` — 60s of 183s (33% of the whole macapp unit suite)

**File:** `macapp/WorkroomAppTests/WorkroomStatusTests.swift:877-978`

`GatedGHRunner.run()` (line 975) does `try? await Task.sleep(nanoseconds: 60_000_000_000)`.
`GitHubAuthCache`/the probe machinery is deliberately single-flight, so cancelling the test's
wrapper `Task` does NOT cancel the shared in-flight probe — `await task.value` (line 892) blocks
until the full 60s sleep actually finishes, every single run, in CI or locally. Verified by
reading the full test body and the runner double — the mechanism is exactly as measured.

**Fix:** shrink the sleep to ~2-3s (still comfortably longer than the 2s poll-for-entry window
the test itself uses at line 886-889 to detect the probe has started). Update the stale comment
at line 973-974 ("long enough that the test's own deadline fails first if cancellation never
propagates") to match the new duration/margin — leaving it unchanged after the sleep shrinks
would misdocument the safety margin for the next person who touches this file. The assertion
(`store.githubCLIStatus` unchanged after cancellation) is legitimate and must be kept exactly as
is — this is a real regression guard (header comment: "the false, sticky 'GitHub CLI not signed
in'" bug), just do not shrink the sleep so much it races the runner's own `enteredGHProbe` gate.

**Impact: saves ~57-58s of the 183s macapp unit suite. Bigger than every other finding in this
plan combined.** Also explains why parallelism work didn't help — XCTest parallelizes per class,
and a hardcoded 60s sleep inside one class floors that class's wall-clock regardless of how many
workers run alongside it.

### B. Fixed-duration `settle()` busy-wait helper, duplicated across 4 files (~17-20s)

**Files (verified via grep, one more than the original survey found):**
- `macapp/WorkroomAppTests/ChangedFileRowInvalidationTests.swift`
- `macapp/WorkroomAppTests/HistoryRowInvalidationTests.swift`
- `macapp/WorkroomAppTests/DiffViewerLazyRenderingTests.swift`
- `macapp/WorkroomAppTests/AgentResumeCoordinatorTests.swift` (not in the original survey — found by grepping `func settle` across the test dir; same anti-pattern, called ~6 times with a 0.5s default)

Each defines a private `settle(seconds:)` that busy-waits a FIXED duration regardless of how fast
the thing being waited on actually converges:
```swift
private func settle(_ view: NSView, seconds: TimeInterval = 0.6) {
  let deadline = Date().addingTimeInterval(seconds)
  while Date() < deadline {
    view.layoutSubtreeIfNeeded()
    RunLoop.current.run(until: Date().addingTimeInterval(0.02))
  }
  view.layoutSubtreeIfNeeded()
}
```
This always pays the full `seconds` argument — it's not a poll-until-condition with an early
exit, it's a poll-until-timeout. `ChangedFileRowInvalidationTests` alone calls it 3x for a
guaranteed 2.4s minimum, matching its measured 3.1s almost exactly.

**Fix:** keep the assertions (these are real regression nets for named App Hangs —
WORKROOM-2B/2T/2S per the doc comments, cross-referenced in project memory
`macapp-focus-responder-apphang-2t.md`). Per review decision, extract ONE shared helper instead of
patching 4 private copies (DRY — the 4 files currently duplicate the anti-pattern, patching each
in place would duplicate the fix too): add `macapp/WorkroomAppTests/Support/Settle.swift`, an
`XCTestCase` extension taking a closure returning the convergence signal, polling it with an

# Plan: cut test-suite runtime — defect fixes + genuine superfluous-test cuts

## Context

Test suite is slow. Prior attempt to speed it up at the infra/parallelism level failed, so the
ask was to instead find tests that are superfluous, unnecessary, or testing something this app
doesn't actually provide, and cut/consolidate those.

Three parallel Explore agents surveyed the Go CLI tests, the macapp Swift unit tests, and the
macapp XCUITest suite. I then verified their highest-impact claims by reading the actual source
(not just trusting agent summaries) — several claims didn't hold up and are corrected below,
because a review's value is worthless if the recommendations are wrong.
